raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to solve perceived limitations of permanent metallic drug-eluting stents (DES): chronic caging, impaired vasomotion, late inflammation, difficulties with future bypass grafting or repeat PCI, and persistent risk of very late events. The leading concept was “vascular restoration therapy,” in which a temporary antiproliferative scaffold would provide early radial support and drug delivery, then disappear, potentially leaving a more physiologic vessel [1]. Early first-in-human studies of the poly-L-lactic acid everolimus-eluting Absorb BVS showed feasibility, low early event rates, and late lumen enlargement with return of vasomotion signals, generating substantial enthusiasm [2], [3]. Second-generation iterations improved radial strength and drug delivery but retained relatively thick struts, limited expansion range, and prolonged resorption kinetics [4], [5].

Randomized evidence initially appeared encouraging. ABSORB II, ABSORB III, ABSORB Japan, and ABSORB China generally demonstrated non-inferiority for composite clinical endpoints at 1 year when compared with cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents, although point estimates often favored metallic DES [6], [7], [8], [9]. Smaller comparative studies, including EVERBIO II and TROFI II, extended experience to broader elective PCI and ST-elevation myocardial infarction populations, suggesting that acute procedural success was achievable in selected lesions [10], [11]. However, as follow-up accrued, a consistent safety signal emerged: excess target-lesion failure, target-vessel myocardial infarction, and definite or probable scaffold thrombosis, especially between 1 and 3 years, the period during which dismantling and resorption occur [12], [13].

Meta-analyses clarified the magnitude and consistency of this hazard. Patient-level and trial-level analyses showed that Absorb BVS was associated with higher scaffold thrombosis and repeat revascularization than contemporary everolimus-eluting metallic stents, with the absolute risk amplified in small vessels and complex lesions [14], [15], [16]. A broad network meta-analysis similarly found inferior safety versus best-in-class DES, undermining the rationale for routine implantation [17]. Importantly, the comparator was a moving target: metallic DES had become thinner, more deliverable, more biocompatible, and extremely safe, reducing the margin for a bulkier temporary device to show incremental clinical value.

Mechanistic investigations identified several converging causes. Thick struts disturbed flow and delayed endothelial coverage; suboptimal lesion preparation or undersizing left malapposed struts; overexpansion risked fracture; and late scaffold discontinuity could protrude into the lumen during resorption [18], [19]. Registries of scaffold thrombosis highlighted underexpansion, malapposition, incomplete lesion coverage, and very late structural discontinuity as recurrent findings on optical coherence tomography [20]. These observations led to the “PSP” implantation paradigm—adequate predilatation, appropriate vessel sizing, and high-pressure post-dilatation—which improved acute scaffold geometry and may reduce early adverse events [21], [22]. Nevertheless, technique could not fully negate intrinsic limitations of thick-strut polymer scaffolds, narrow expansion latitude, and slow bioresorption.

Clinical practice therefore changed rapidly. Regulatory warnings and market withdrawal of Absorb in many regions transformed BVS from a mainstream aspiration into a cautionary technology. Professional consensus emphasized restriction to controlled studies, meticulous imaging-guided implantation, avoidance of small vessels, and prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy when polymeric scaffolds had been used [23]. Long-term follow-up reinforced this position: excess device-related events attenuated after expected resorption but did not translate into a clear late clinical advantage over metallic DES [24], [25].

The field did not disappear. Magnesium-based sirolimus-eluting absorbable metal scaffolds were designed to offer thinner struts, more predictable degradation, and better acute mechanical behavior than PLLA platforms. BIOSOLVE studies showed promising safety and performance, though without definitive proof of superiority over contemporary DES [26], [27]. Other polymeric platforms, including DESolve and radiopaque tyrosine-derived polycarbonate scaffolds, demonstrated technical feasibility but remained constrained by limited randomized data and evolving commercial viability [28], [29]. These programs underscore that “bioresorbable” is not a single class effect; mechanical design, strut thickness, degradation chemistry, drug kinetics, and implantation protocol all determine outcomes.

For current PCI, metallic DES remain the standard of care for most patients because they combine excellent deliverability, low restenosis, and very low thrombosis rates. Bioresorbable scaffolds retain conceptual appeal in younger patients, long diffuse disease, bifurcations requiring future access, and settings where restoration of vasomotion might matter, but these advantages remain largely unproven clinically. Future success will require thinner struts, broader expansion tolerance, rapid endothelialization, predictable resorption without dismantling, imaging-compatible markers, and randomized trials powered for patient-centered endpoints against contemporary ultrathin DES [30]. The BVS experience has been scientifically valuable: it showed that disappearance alone is insufficient, and that temporary coronary scaffolding must be safer than a permanent implant before theoretical late benefits can matter.
